messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm attempting to do distance sampling with trail cameras now and am having trouble figuring out how to factor in the amount of time the cameras are set for. I have the Howe paper but cannot figure out how they did that. This is on the island of Guam and we have high Philippine deer and feral pig densities. I assume on the distance software this would be in the "sampling fraction" which is where you account for the field of view in the cameras. Is this correct?

Scott

messages.body_plain:
Scott

Good to hear from you; I remember you from a training workshop here in St Andrews 4 or 5 years ago.

There are two components to your question:
how is effort recorded, in the case of Howe's work, effort is the number of snapshot moments recorded by the camera divided by the recycle time of the shutter.  As they say in their paper:
We predetermine a ﬁnite set of snapshot moments within T _k , t units of time apart, at which an image of an animal could be obtained. Temporal eﬀort at the point is then T _k /t.
The second component is the proportion of the surrounding habitat over which the camera can detect animals.  This is the quantity theta/(2 x pi) described in the paper.  Assuming this quantity is the same for all cameras, the quantity theta/(2 x pi) can be entered as a multiplier (in Distance for Windows) or the argument sampling_fraction when working in R.
Hope that helps.

Eric Rexstad
Senior Research Fellow, CREEM, Univ. of St Andrews, Charity SC013532

messages.body_plain:
Eden

I agree with your concluding statement "It doesn't seem as though these covariates will affect my estimates or provide a better model".  From the extensive summary table you provided, you will see the estimates of P_a for most of your models are only changing in the second or third decimal, meaning the estimates of abundance are robust to model choice for this data set.  That is a desirable situation for any analyst.  Consequently, you should be able to live without adjustment terms in addition to covariates in the detection function.

But in answer to your question: how can I fit a model with both adjustment terms and covariates.  The answer is you cannot do that with the R package Distance .  If you really want to fit such models, you will need to use the Distance for Windows software.  Recognise that if you do want both covariates and adjustment terms, you will have additional analysis decisions to make regarding scaling of perpendicular distances by sigma or by truncation distance.  I refer you to Section 3.3.2 of Buckland et al. (2004) or Marques and Buckland (2003).

The reason this type of model cannot be fitted using the R software is that it is numerically difficult to do.  Optimisation problems commonly arise in fitting such models.  The optimisation method in Distance for Windows has been tuned to cope with such situations.

Why are such models cause numerical difficulties?  A simple explanation is that in detection function modelling, covariates and adjustment terms are each trying to perform a similar task:  improve fit of the key function model to the data.  Covariates and adjustment terms contain similar information about the shape of the detection function; this causes anxiety for optimisation methods.

Marques, F. F. C., and S. T. Buckland. 2003. Incorporating covariates into standard line transect analyses. Biometrics 59: 924–935. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341x.2003.00107.x.

Eric Rexstad

messages.body_plain:
Scott, you can’t treat camera trap data like normal point transect data because of animal movement.  If you leave a camera at the point for a long time, eventually, animals will come close enough to be detected.  But if you take ‘snapshots’ at fixed periods of time, then that eliminates the bias from animal movement.  Each snapshot corresponds to a visit to the point in conventional point transect sampling.  So effort is number of snapshots – multiplied by the fraction of the circle covered by the camera’s sensor.  If snapshots are defined independently of animals, then you can choose the time between snapshots to be anything you want.  Non-independence becomes more of an issue the shorter you make the time between snapshots, so you need analysis methods that are robust to non-independence.  If the camera is triggered by animal movement, then more care is needed in choosing time between snapshots.  If you make this time large, you will overestimate abundance, because your snapshot sequences will always start with an animal present.  So the time needs to be such that animals will not normally pass through the sector covered by the sensor in a shorter time than the one you select.  For many animals, something of the order of 1-5 seconds might work OK.  If you take say 2 seconds, then you have to include in your effort the time the camera is operating divided by 2 seconds – in other words, you’ll have a ‘snapshot’ every 2 seconds, whether or not an animal has triggered the sensor, and choosing a short time ensures that any bias caused by having a snapshot whenever the sensor is triggered ensures any bias will be very small.

I hope that clarifies.

Steve Buckland

Is it, therefore, advisable to implement point transect survey in examining the area since it most likely reflects the nature of the operation.

Anthony

This is a question with a number of sub-questions.  A couple of questions related to study design, rather than distance sampling, that I'll leave unanswered: a) has there been surveys performed in the oil field prior to the commencement of human activity or b) are there areas being surveyed that are outside the field where development is occurring?  To make some statements about "impact" it needs to be related to something that might be "unimpacted".  Furthermore, if the platform from which the survey is to be conducted is a "DP pilelay vessel", it sounds as if it may be the cause of the anthropogenic stress you are trying to investigate.  That will make assessment of the impact difficult (if animals are actively evading the survey vessel).

Finally coming onto distance sampling issues.  If the vessel is stationary or moving very slowly, it may well more closely resemble a point transect survey rather than a line transect survey.  Unfortunately, distance sampling methods are sensitive to animal movement.  When the surveyor is moving slowly or not at all, methods will likely overestimate abundance because animals will eventually move into the field of view if the ship is stationary for sufficiently long.

One way to avoid the effect of movement is to conduct a cue count survey, where you are estimating the density of cues, then incorporating information about cue production rate per individual, to estimate animal density.  This might work for the pilot whales, where the cue would be blows; but it is unlikely to be helpful for the bottlenose dolphins.  Seems you would be better served, if possible, to have an alternative platform that a) moves faster than the study animals and b) is not engaged in laying pipes.

We discuss and demonstrate the analysis of whale blow cue count surveys in our online distance sampling training materials

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch6/L6-2%20Multipliers.pdf

messages.body_plain:
Good day Scott, and thanks Eric and Steve,

Scott, regarding your question: "How are the snapshot moments defined/quantified": You define them as specific times of day. You also chose a daily time interval or intervals during which you will measure distances if animals are detected.

It's helpful to plot detection times over the 24-hour day before measuring distances, because you might decide to reduce your daily survey duration to e.g. near dawn and dusk for crepuscular species or daylight hours for diurnal species (as in our article), and there's no need to measure distances to animals detected outside of this interval.

Also choose a value for t (duration of time step between snapshot moments). If t = 3, you could define moments as e.g. 0, 3, 6..., 57 seconds after the even minute, OR as 2, 5, 8,..., etc. seconds after the even minute, in real time. Moments are the same for all cameras. Regardless of when a camera is triggered, distances are measured only at these moments.

Tk is the total number of seconds a camera operates at location k. It's convenient to define a daily Tk, in seconds. This is the "time interval during which you will measure distances" above, so it might be less than the number of seconds in 24 hours; it might be the number of seconds within a 2- or 12-hour period. Multiply this by the number of days a camera operated and could have detected animals at a location to obtain Tk at that location. Then, dividing Tk by t (both in seconds) gives you the total number of opportunities to detect an animal at a location over the duration of a survey. This is your temporal effort at that location. Enter it as "Effort" in software IFF you are quantifying spatial effort < than a circle using a multiplier or the sampling_fraction argument. Alternatively, you can avoid multipliers and calculate Effort as described in the article (incorporating both spatial and temporal components)..

Note that if we detected one animal at every opportunity, the encounter rate would be 1.0. In practice, encounter rates (detections per opportunity) are very low with camera trap point transects, because we observe no animals during most opportunities.

Hope this helps,
Eric H

Scott

A few more things to think about.

You say your time period will be "night" therefore 8 hours; but which 8 hour period.  Defining the end points of the time period will be critical for animals with crepuscular activity patterns--moving the end points just a bit will alter the encounter rate.  Similarly recognise changing the time interval between snapshot moments will have an effect upon your effort, hence your estimates.  You'll need to be able to defend both decisions.

The sampling fraction multiplier is viewing angle of camera divided by degrees (360) or radians (2*pi) in a complete circle.

Hi All,

Quite often when I add a covariate (e.g. seastate, migration etc) in Rdistance, the hazard rate detection function sufficiently improves the AIC, but also significantly increases estimated N (sometimes by 1000’s from observations of only couple hundred). I remember reading in the Review paper of Distance by Thomas et al., 2010 that Hazard Rate model can often fit implausible shapes, especially for spiked data (which from exploratory analysis, I believe my data is). I am struggling to choose between a hazard rate model which has a much lower AIC but significantly increases estimated N (and has a much lower estimated PA) or a half normal model which has an AIC of at least 10 higher than HR, and seems to underestimate N. If anyone could shed any light on this, I would be very grateful.

Thanks,
Raph

Is it ok to compute a single detection function, and then apply them separately during the DSM stage? Or is it still best to have separate detection functions for each year?

Thanks for your help

Eliphaleth

Thanks for the questions and happy you found the vignettes we have posted.  Now to your questions.

Dealing with potential bias in density of individuals is indeed most readily accomplished by incorporating group size into the detection function.  This explicitly recognises that detectability is a function of group size as well as distance from the transect.  The approach described in the "group size" vignette that you reference does exactly that.
There is not a way to select mean group size at the global level for stratum-level density estimates.  I'm not sure this is a good idea because if you want density estimates at the stratum level, it would seem that stratum-level mean group size would be the appropriate thing to use.
There is a function dht2 released to CRAN in January that enables post-stratification at the observation level.  I don't think we have an example of its use on the examples web page, but have a look at the documentation for the dht2 function in the Distance package.  You can also get a clue from slide 15 of this talk: https://workshops.distancesampling.org/standrews-2019/intro/lectures/BlockG-stratification.pdf

Eric Rexstad

That's a good observation on your part, recognising that the hazard rate model, in some circumstances, produces large abundance estimates because of its rapid steep decline.  Out of curiosity, how many detections are in the data set you show?  We have seen this behaviour in the hazard rate model for small (<30) data sets.

AIC is used as a guide in model selection; it is not the only criterion to be used.  The analyst needs to also incorporate biological plausibility into their model selection decisions.  The figure you present suggests that average detectability is estimated to be ~0.2 at 100m (don't know units?).  In some circumstances that may be biologically plausible (ants in the jungle); in other situations (blue whales in the ocean) that may be quite unreasonable.  Without knowing more about the study that gave rise to the data, it is hard to say more.

Thanks for your quick response. Looking through this forum has been very useful, with many of the previous questions and responses answering a lot of things that were on my mind!

In this particular example, the study was a set of line transects capturing distribution of whales, during different migration periods and over several years. I decided to truncate at the 85th percentile but wasn't sure whether truncating even further would limit the model due to the (smallish) sample size already. What I have just noticed however, the graph above shows the detection function with ~as.factor(Migration) as a covariate - could it be that i am getting such a graph, because of the different amount of observations per migration (i.e. Northern migration may have 23 compared to southern migration with 34 observations and hence dataset is small).

Saying this, however, I get similar results with different years that have larger datasets (even when i have pooled all observations across all the years, my Hazard Rate detectability doesn't seem to get much bigger than 0.6 at 100m). One option is using a half normal, however the differences in estimated abundance between the two makes me question myself.

Whilst we are on the subject of AIC and gof, I have noticed when I pool all years together, with more observations, many of my models have a CmV P value of less than 0.05 indicating no model fit. However, this may be due to the larger sample size (although still only~250 observations). So, is it then better to choose a model with a p-value that is above 0.05 or still be inclined with choosing the model with the lower AIC, even if it has a p value < 0.05 indicating no model fit? I hope this question makes sense.

Thanks for your time,

Raph

Good day Scott,
Re: activity period. Rowcliffe et al 2014 described methods for estimating the proportion of time active at camera height (and so available for detection by CTs), directly from times of detection, within any time interval (e.g. 24, 12, or 8 hours). There's an R package 'activity'. This can help you select daily Tk, and also account for temporally limited availability for detection within Tk.

Selection of t is a trade-off between missed observations of e.g. fast-moving animals close to the camera (missed if t is too large - no bias but costs you data), and data management (at some point, more observations of the same animals at almost the same location just creates more work measuring distances, without improving precision). Also, with smaller t, trigger speed and unavoidable delays between recordings could start to cause slight bias. Optimal values haven't been identified, and would likely vary across species and camera placements.

Eric H

I've seen a few errors regarding using unary operators, and convergence issues in some of my other models - does anyone have an explanation for what the root of these errors are?

Elling, it’s not so much that the hazard-rate fit that is odd, it’s just trying to fit your data, and those data are odd.  You have a huge spike at or near zero.  You need to understand what causes that.  Are there problems with distance estimation?  Or are you getting perpendicular distances from radial distances plus angles, with many angles rounded to zero?  Or is detection probability extremely variable, with some animals only detectable very close to the line, and others detectable at large distances?  With these data, you certainly need to truncate, and you’ll probably need to truncate substantially more than 15% of your data, given how long the tail of the distribution is.

It's important to realise that in your analyses, g(0)=1 by assumption, so your statement of ‘approx 0.3 sightability at g(0)’ is incorrect.  But your data have such a sharp fall-off that the flexible hazard-rate model has to fall extremely rapidly from one to fit your data, while the half-normal model makes little attempt to fit the distances close to zero.  Unfortunately, with such data, reliable estimation is unlikely to be possible.  If the problem with your data is caused by failure of an assumption, then you need to address this for future surveys.  If you believe this is not the issue, try plotting the histogram with more intervals, especially having several intervals spanning the first 100 (m?) or so, to see the pattern of fall-off very close to the line.  It is not possible to advise on appropriate analysis here without much more detail about the study, and why the data are so problematic.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Elling, you don’t say what the study species is.  In addition to the issues you mention, could animals be attracted to the line, e.g. to ride the bow wave?  Yes, probably better to exclude narrow straits from your area when you try to estimate abundance.  Possibly any areas with a high density of icebergs too.  In both cases, you may have quite extreme departure from the assumption that animals are uniformly distributed with distance from the line.

In my experience, angles quite a lot larger than 5 deg can be rounded to zero.  If an animal is seen, observers tend to try to follow the animal.  By the time they record distance and angle, they may have lost the animal, and have only a vague idea of where it was.  Careful training, and a protocol for dealing with issues like this, can help.  Many years ago, when I first got involved in this type of survey, Antarctic minke whale surveys consistently showed a spike in the data like yours.  The problem was angles rounded to zero.  The next year, the message got through, so observers rounded instead to either 2 or 3 deg, and the problem was just as severe!  Angle boards were introduced in an effort to improve estimates, to no avail – the crew, who had lots of experience searching for whales on whaling vessels, didn’t consider they needed the boards.  So next time, the chief scientist overseeing the cruise took part in the distance and angle experiments that had been set up to try to resolve the problem.  He out-performed all of the experienced crew members, after which they used the angle boards, and the problem disappeared completely.  Your circumstances may be very different, but it is worth considering how the observers operate.

You say you have distance=0 for a large proportion of observations.  Look at how many of those have a radial distance of zero.  If a high proportion, then the problem is animals being attracted to the vessel.  In this case, you need observers to be detecting animals before they respond to the ship – which may be problematic.  If most of the zeros are a result of the angle being recorded as zero, then I suspect the error in angle estimates is substantially larger than you realise.

Sorry not to be more helpful.

Steve

Back in the 1980s, we developed ‘smearing’ to try to reduce the effect of rounding angles to zero.  It was never very successful, largely because a proportion of sightings appeared to be recorded as zero angle when the real angle was substantially larger.  My guess is that this occurred when there was a brief sighting that was not resighted, and the delay in recording an angle meant that the observer was unsure of the original location, and tended to record zero angle if it was somewhere ahead.  You can easily test your belief that zero angles were in reality no larger than 5.  Simulate some data with a reasonable pattern of search effort (simulating from a 2-dimensional hazard-rate model would be ideal), and see if you get as spiked a distribution as for your real data, if angles up to 5 are rounded to zero.  I would be very surprised if you do …

You might also want to look at whether the proportion of zero angles varies appreciably by observer – it’s quite possible that the accuracy of recording varies by observer.

When you have non-random transect lines, it may be worth considering fitting a density surface model, where it is less critical that lines are located independently of the animals.

Anyway, I hope you find a way to utilise your data fully.

Steve

messages.subject_clean: Camera trap distance sampling: Survey effort, survey design, and sample distribution
messages.body_plain:
Background on required effort estimation

We are looking to establish a multi-species monitoring
program across multiple adjacent protected areas. (I am assuming with would
approach each site separately, as they have different habitats and areas, and likely
differ in the detection functions; we also don’t have enough cameras to survey
more than 2 areas at a time. This is a slightly different issue to my main
questions below, so let’s assume we’re talking about a single site here.)

We have a set number of cameras available. We know around 30
terrestrial species are present, all of which are possible to capture with the
same camera trap set up. We have encounter rates/capture rates from a study in
one site from around 7 years ago (Suzuki et al. 2017), which used targeted camera
placement.

I have taken the encounter rates from this study, reducing
them to possible encounter rates with random/systematic placement (non-targeted)
based on differences seen between targeted and non-targeted in Cusack et al
2015 (https://dx.doi.org/10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0126373,
mean of 2.26) and Kolowski & Forrester 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0186679,
max of 9.7). I have used these values, along with the number of cameras and
desired number of captures (based on Howe et al. 2017 and Besson et al. 2020)
to give rough estimates the number of days effort required.

I have also approached this from another direction, using
Equation 7.1 from Buckland et al. 1999 to estimate the effort needed for a
defined coefficient of variation. And finally using equations from page 305 of
Buckland et al. 1999 to estimate CV per species based on a defined number of
days.

These various estimates all roughly converge, suggesting
that to get estimates for around 6 of the most common potential target species with
a reasonable CV, we will need to survey for a minimum of 6 months with the
number of cameras we have available. I’ve attached the Excel used for this, but
it is intended just for internal use so might not be easy to follow.

Question

Whilst these estimations can give total effort, they don’t
inform survey design. For example, if we had 50 cameras available, we could
distribute them systematically across our total sample area in a grid, and
leave them for 6 months. This would give the same total effort as splitting the
survey around into e.g. 6 subareas, and deploying 50 cameras in subarea each
for 1 month, then moving them all to the next subarea. This latter approach would
increase the camera density (but also logistical costs), but I’m not clear on
what the advantage of that is with distance sampling. If our sampling points
are systematically distributed, and are representative of the habitat, what
benefit does increasing density offer? With some sampling methods (e.g. SECR)
we need animals to be captured on multiple cameras, so a high density is
required. I don’t think this is an assumption of CTDS, but Besson et al. 2020 found
that precision increased with higher number of sites with at least one capture.
I’m not clear if this is an increase in proportion of cameras with at least one
capture, or if it is an absolute increase (e.g. is 10/100 the same precision as
10/50, and that 15/100 and 15/50 offers the same increase in precision).

The sub-area approach is used by Besson et al. 2020, but
Appendix S1 discussed design limitations of not surveying the whole area. They discuss
an assumption that sampling locations need to be spaced larger than the home range
of the target species, to avoid double detections. I also wonder if the survey
was designed and implemented without CTDS in mind, as it was begun in 2016.

This post is getting long, so let me summarise with a couple
of questions I’m struggling with:

1.
How can we estimate a minimum required camera
density across a site to ensure representation? Is it based on habitat heterogeneity,
or species home ranges?

2.
Does increasing camera density, whilst keeping
the same total effort, improve estimates? If so, how could we calculate the
optimum density to balance with practicality? (An infinite density of cameras
would presumably give perfect estimation (a count) but is also slightly beyond
our limited budgets…)

3.
Answers to 1 and 2 would probably answer this as
well, but just to be explicit and help my understanding: is a sub-area
approach, increasing camera density with the same total effort, such as in
Besson et al. 2020, optimum for CTDS? If so, what considerations are needed to
avoid bias (e.g. avoiding temporal or other gradients by ordering the surveying
of subareas randomly)?

Thanks as always for your valuable insights!

My understanding of the method is that yes, lingering animals are counted as multiple encounters.  In principle, this method does not require identification of animals, so knowing whether it is the same animal is not possible in all circumstances.

You are correct that multiple detections can cause overdispersion in the data leading to challenges with model selection as all detections are assumed independent.  There is a paper by Eric, Steve and others that addresses this issue:

All good questions Olly.  I don't know that there has been much work done regarding survey design for CTDS methods; I'll let others correct me.  I can't speak to rotational designs, which I suspect the Beeson et al. (2020) approach uses.

One thing I noted in the Howe et al. (2017) duiker study is the considerable variation in encounter rates between their 23 camera stations.  As Howe et al. (2017) point out, over 99% of the variance in their estimate of duiker density was attributable to encounter rate variation between stations.  I think the survey design lesson there is to consider habitat quality and perhaps contemplate stratified designs as well as have large numbers of cameras to estimate the encounter rate variance well.

On Jun 17 2020, at 4:11 am, Olly Griffin <ogri...@wcs.org> wrote:

> Background on required effort estimation
>
> We are looking to establish a multi-species monitoring program across multiple adjacent protected areas. (I am assuming with would approach each site separately, as they have different habitats and areas, and likely differ in the detection functions; we also don’t have enough cameras to survey more than 2 areas at a time. This is a slightly different issue to my main questions below, so let’s assume we’re talking about a single site here.)
>
> We have a set number of cameras available. We know around 30 terrestrial species are present, all of which are possible to capture with the same camera trap set up. We have encounter rates/capture rates from a study in one site from around 7 years ago (Suzuki et al. 2017), which used targeted camera placement.
>
> I have taken the encounter rates from this study, reducing them to possible encounter rates with random/systematic placement (non-targeted) based on differences seen between targeted and non-targeted in Cusack et al 2015 (https://dx.doi.org/10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0126373, mean of 2.26) and Kolowski & Forrester 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0186679, max of 9.7). I have used these values, along with the number of cameras and desired number of captures (based on Howe et al. 2017 and Besson et al. 2020) to give rough estimates the number of days effort required.
>
> I have also approached this from another direction, using Equation 7.1 from Buckland et al. 1999 to estimate the effort needed for a defined coefficient of variation. And finally using equations from page 305 of Buckland et al. 1999 to estimate CV per species based on a defined number of days.
>
> These various estimates all roughly converge, suggesting that to get estimates for around 6 of the most common potential target species with a reasonable CV, we will need to survey for a minimum of 6 months with the number of cameras we have available. I’ve attached the Excel used for this, but it is intended just for internal use so might not be easy to follow.
>
> Question
>
> Whilst these estimations can give total effort, they don’t inform survey design. For example, if we had 50 cameras available, we could distribute them systematically across our total sample area in a grid, and leave them for 6 months. This would give the same total effort as splitting the survey around into e.g. 6 subareas, and deploying 50 cameras in subarea each for 1 month, then moving them all to the next subarea. This latter approach would increase the camera density (but also logistical costs), but I’m not clear on what the advantage of that is with distance sampling. If our sampling points are systematically distributed, and are representative of the habitat, what benefit does increasing density offer? With some sampling methods (e.g. SECR) we need animals to be captured on multiple cameras, so a high density is required. I don’t think this is an assumption of CTDS, but Besson et al. 2020 found that precision increased with higher number of sites with at least one capture. I’m not clear if this is an increase in proportion of cameras with at least one capture, or if it is an absolute increase (e.g. is 10/100 the same precision as 10/50, and that 15/100 and 15/50 offers the same increase in precision).
>
> The sub-area approach is used by Besson et al. 2020, but Appendix S1 discussed design limitations of not surveying the whole area. They discuss an assumption that sampling locations need to be spaced larger than the home range of the target species, to avoid double detections. I also wonder if the survey was designed and implemented without CTDS in mind, as it was begun in 2016.
>
> This post is getting long, so let me summarise with a couple of questions I’m struggling with:
>
> 1.      How can we estimate a minimum required camera density across a site to ensure representation? Is it based on habitat heterogeneity, or species home ranges?
>
> 2.      Does increasing camera density, whilst keeping the same total effort, improve estimates? If so, how could we calculate the optimum density to balance with practicality? (An infinite density of cameras would presumably give perfect estimation (a count) but is also slightly beyond our limited budgets…)
>
> 3.      Answers to 1 and 2 would probably answer this as well, but just to be explicit and help my understanding: is a sub-area approach, increasing camera density with the same total effort, such as in Besson et al. 2020, optimum for CTDS? If so, what considerations are needed to avoid bias (e.g. avoiding temporal or other gradients by ordering the surveying of subareas randomly)?
>
> Thanks as always for your valuable insights!
>

Good day Scott,

As Eric and Steve mention, we accept and include non-independent observations. If its midpoint is visible, and the time is within Tk and during a snapshot moment, we record distance and include the observations. It doesn't cause cause bias because a single animal can only be detected once per location per snapshot moment.

The issue with apparent heaping is potentially more complicated. Measuring distances to "resting" animals caused problems in simulations, because an animal that remains in front of the camera can contribute large numbers of observations, and if they are at moderate to far distances, decreasing functions may not fit the data well. Our (imperfect) solution was to avoid sampling during times when animals "rest".

Animals that are awake and moving slightly (thus triggering the sensor) but not going anywhere could cause the same effect, and we don't have a clear reason to sensor the observations (the animal is "active").

I would suggest checking the times of day when cameras detected these lingering animals, and see if they are similar. If there are specific times of day when animals are at their most mobile (e.g. crepuscular?), such that animals detected at these times pass by the camera (often contributing > 1, but not dozens or hundreds, of observations) rather than lingering in front of it, then you could limit Tk to these times. That could exclude most or all lingering animals from the data, improving fit without causing bias.

Bessone et al. (2020) sensored observations of animals obviously reacting to the camera, and this improved fit (another imperfect solution to a similar problem).   https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2664.13602.

If you had only one animal that lingered in front of a camera and this animal created a "bump" in the observed distances far from 0, you could just say so and exclude the animal or most of the observations it contributed.

Eric

messages.body_plain:
Good day Olly,

There is potentially a lot to talk about here. I'll start by trying to answer your 3 questions.

1.      How can we estimate a minimum required camera density across a site to ensure representation? Is it based on habitat heterogeneity, or species home ranges?

I don't know how to estimate minimum or optimum camera density. However, precision will certainly improve as more cameras are deployed within a fixed area for a fixed duration.

If you are interested in average density across an entire region of interest, you could deploy cameras throughout according to a randomized design. They could be moved e.g. once, twice, or not at all. I'd recommend at least 100 sampling locations, so if you had 50 cameras, you could move them to new locations once during the survey, rather than relying on only 50 small sampling locations spread over a large area (sensitive to camera placement at a fine scale).

If differences in density among sub-regions is of key interest, you might want to sample each one intensively, one or two at a time.

I think that in theory, if two points fall within the home range of the same animal, those points should not be considered independent, so wide spacing is often recommended. Multiple closely-spaced CTs could be treated as a single point when estimating variance. However, with CTDS, we violate the independence assumption within points, and use adjusted or robust methods for selecting among models and estimating variance. Even if points are closely-spaced, animals can only be detected at one location during a single snapshot moment, so I'm not sure how much it matters if multiple points fall within the range of a single species.

2.      Does increasing camera density, whilst keeping the same total effort, improve estimates? If so, how could we calculate the optimum density to balance with practicality? (An infinite density of cameras would presumably give perfect estimation (a count) but is also slightly beyond our limited budgets…)

Yes, very likely. Variances increase with increasing variation in numbers of observations of animals across points, so with more points, variances should be lower. This becomes increasingly important as animals use their habitat more non-randomly. E.g if we survey one habitat in the wet season, and another in the dry, do results reflect seasonal movements or behaviour rather than abundance? Hi All,

Apologies for asking another question so soon. After having read some of the responses on this group, I have tried to gear my questions so that they address what I have not yet seen. I am modelling DSM over a grid cell of 500mx500m. My segment length is currently at 5km (which is at least twice the truncation distance of the detection function, and also not so long that it affects my spatial distribution with depth as a possible covariate). I aim to produce separate density surface models for cetaceans over two areas (A1 and A2) for three years of study. I am using the tweedie response variable due to overdispersion of zero data. I am using a detection function which has been obtained from pooling three years of study together, to fit a DSM for each year separately. I have read parts of Wood’s second edition introduction to GAM, which, although my brain hurts a little, has been very useful.

I am mostly interested in spatial distribution within a study area, and am not extrapolating outside the area, so a smooth of location (s(x,y)) is a good term to start with. I have also tried adding Depth to models as a smooth term to see if this improves.  From what I gather, if a significance of smooth p-value tends to 1, this should be removed from the model. Hi Raph, hi listfolk,

Quick reply to your three questions:

- On p-values: bear in mind the test p-value is for. It's asking
(roughly), "is this smooth different from a line at 0". Graphically: can
you draw a straight line through the confidence band around the smooth.
A non-significant p-value might be because the term is unrelated to the
counts you saw or just because there is a lot of uncertainty around that
smooth. If a smooth of space is not significant and you don't have other
terms in the model, that might be an indication that your data don't
require a spatial model (since their distribution doesn't seem to vary
in space).

- If REML is used you cannot compare REML scores. BUT you can compare AIC.

- Spike at lag 1 in the correlogram means that segments that are direct
neighbours (either side) are correlated. I'm less of a fan of these
diagnostics as I think they're often a bit hard to interpret, you might
find the practical solutions from the recent spatial modelling course
here useful: http://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-dsm-2020/ in
particular the part on model checking may help.

Hope this is useful!

cheers,

messages.body_plain:
Dear Helpful Distance Sampling People

Please can you assist with this query.

I wish to understand which measure, as reported by software distance, to use for comparing z-tests or t-tests of significant differences of density estimates.

As context: I have a line transect data set which is stratified by 5 habitats and 3 years – i.e. 15 strata.

There are a total of 1,439 observations, between these strata.  The number of observations per strata is unequal: the range is from 2 to 322, averaging 95 per strata.

In the Introduction to Distance Sampling 2001 book, it suggests on pp 76 to 77 and 84 to 85 to use z or t tests based on the variance of D.

However – please what is the variance of D – where is this reported in software distance?

I am not sure this is the same as the Standard Error of the density estimate D.

p76 of the book suggests variance is the square root of the Standard Error.

My aspiration would be to then use an R function such as aovSufficient (HH package) to then conduct pairwise ANOVA tests between strata.   That particular package requires n (observations), standard dev and  mean.    I don’t know that SE is the same as sd, when we are talking distance sampling.

A related point: the strata are analysed with a pooled global detection function.   Does this prompt any thought about the independence of the strata estimates, when conducting these significance tests, which would affect how I conduct the comparison z or t test.

Thank you if you can help.

I hope you are all safe and well meanwhile.

Carlos Bedson at the Manchester Metropolitan University, England

Hi Carlos

Happy to see you are still engaged in distance sampling.

Short answer about where to find variance in Distance output:  you've got the relationship between variance and standard error backward:  variance is the square of standard error (not square root).  Here is a clip from some Distance output:

If the standard error of the density estimate is 0.48578, then the variance of the density estimate is 0.23598  (the square of 0.48578).

But you make an important point about the sample size in some strata being small.  Because of that, you've used a pooled detection function across strata.  You correctly note that because of the pooled detection function, those stratum-specific estimates are not independent.

The way to deal with that non-independence is described in Section 3.6.5 of Buckland et al. (2001).  Between equations 3.105 and 3.106 on p.85, the non-independent issue is discussed and the remainder of the section and equations therein describe how to proceed when a pooled detection function is involved in the density comparison.

If you get stuck with the calculations, contact me off-list, I can walk you through them.

Eric Rexstad

Mark recapture distance sampling training workshop

Registration is now open for our latest online interactive training
workshop, on mark-recapture distance sampling.  Join us by video from
anywhere around the world!  For full details, and to register, please go to

https://www.creem.st-andrews.ac.uk/mark-recapture-distance-sampling-workshop/

Workshop Overview

Conventional distance sampling methods assume that all animals at zero
distance are detected with certainty.  However, in some situations this
assumption is violated, and some animals are missed, causing a negative
bias in the density and abundance estimates.  This occurs on some
shipboard surveys of marine mammals, for example, where animals may be
missed on the trackline because they are underwater while the survey
vessel passes, or because the sea conditions are rough so that even some
animals right on the line are missed.  The former (being underwater and
so not available for detection) is often called availability bias and
the latter perception bias.

In this two-day workshop, we cover survey protocols and analytical
methods for dealing with both perception bias and availability bias. The
workshop is intended for those already familiar with the basics of
distance sampling.

Instructors

Len Thomas and David Borchers

Timing

24th and 25th August 2020

17:00-19:30 British Summer Time // 12:00-14:30 Eastern Daylight Time
(EDT) // 09:00-11:30 Pacific Daylight Time (PDT)

Enrolment limit

15 participants

Format and delivery method

The workshop will be a mix of live online interactive sessions,
delivered via videoconference software (Microsoft Teams), and computer
exercises.   There will be two sessions in total, on successive days,
with a total class time of 4 hours (including breaks) and an additional
computer exercise to complete after the first day and before the second.
